<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:retract-sober}
Every retract of a sober space is sober.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:T2-co-sober} Every $T_2$-space is co-sober.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a $k$-irreducible compact subset of a Hausdorff space $X$. If $x,y\in K$ are distinct, choose disjoint open sets $U$ and $V$ with $x\in U$ and $y\in V$. Then
\[
  K=(K\setminus U)\cup(K\setminus V).
\]
Both sets on the right are proper compact subsets of $K$, and all subsets are saturated because the space is $T_{1}$. This contradicts $k$-irreducibility. Thus $K$ is a singleton, which is the saturation of its unique point.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:ssturate-closed-co-sober}
Every saturated subspace of a co-sober space is co-sober.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:complete-lattice}
For every complete lattice $L$, the Scott space $\Sigma L$ is sober if and only if $(L,\omega(L))$ is co-sober.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:delete-top}
Let $L$ be a complete lattice with greatest element $1$, and put $L^{-}=L\setminus\{1\}$. Then
\[
  (L,\omega(L))\text{ is co-sober}
  ~\Longleftrightarrow~
  (L^{-},\omega(L^{-}))\text{ is co-sober}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assume that $(L,\omega(L))$ is co-sober. The equality $\omega(L^{-})=\omega(L)|_{L^{-}}$ follows directly from the two subbases. Since the specialization order of $\omega(L)$ is the reverse lattice order, $L^{-}$ is a saturated subspace of $(L,\omega(L))$, and hence by Lemma \ref{lem:ssturate-closed-co-sober}, $(L^{-},\omega(L^{-}))$ is co-sober.

Conversely, suppose that $(L^{-},\omega(L^{-}))$ is co-sober, and let $K$ be a $k$-irreducible compact saturated subset of $(L,\omega(L))$. If $1\in K$, then $K$ is a lower set in the lattice order, and therefore
\[
  K=L=\mathord{\downarrow}_{L}1,
\]
which is the saturation of $1$ in the lower topology. If $1\notin K$, then $K\subseteq L^{-}$. Compactness and saturation pass to the subspace $L^{-}$. Moreover, a compact saturated decomposition of $K$ in $L^{-}$ is also one in $L$, because $L^{-}$ is saturated. Thus $K$ is $k$-irreducible in $L^{-}$ and
\[
  K=\mathord{\downarrow}_{L^{-}}x
\]
for some $x\in L^{-}$. The representing point is unique since the lower topology of a poset is $T_0$. As $x\neq 1$, this set equals $\mathord{\downarrow}_{L}x$. Hence $K$ is principal in $(L,\omega(L))$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theor:bridge}
For every $T_{0}$-space $X$,
\[
  P_{H}(X)\text{ is co-sober}
  ~\Longleftrightarrow~
  \Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)\text{ is sober}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{O}^{-}(X)=\mathcal{O}(X)\setminus\{X\}$. Complementation gives a bijection
\[
  \varphi:\Gamma_{0}(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}^{-}(X),
  ~ \varphi(A)=X\setminus A.
\]
For every proper open set $U$,
$$\begin{array}{lll}
	\varphi(\Diamond U)& =\varphi(\{A\in\Gamma_0 (X) : A\cap U\neq\emptyset\})\\
	           & =\{X\setminus A : A\in\Gamma_0 (X), U\not\subseteq X\setminus A\}\\
	           & =\{V\in\mathcal{O}^{-}(X):U\nsubseteq V\}\\
	           & =\mathcal{O}^{-}(X)\setminus\mathord{\uparrow}U.\\
\end{array}$$
The subbasic set $\Diamond X$ is the whole space. It follows that $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism from $P_{H}(X)$ onto $(\mathcal{O}^{-}(X),\omega(\mathcal{O}^{-}(X)))$.

The lattice $\mathcal{O}(X)$ is complete. Lemma~\ref{lem:delete-top}, followed by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-lattice}, gives
\begin{align*}
  P_{H}(X)\text{ co-sober}
  &\Longleftrightarrow
  (\mathcal{O}^{-}(X),\omega(\mathcal{O}^{-}(X)))\text{ co-sober}\\
  &\Longleftrightarrow
  (\mathcal{O}(X),\omega(\mathcal{O}(X)))\text{ co-sober}\\
  &\Longleftrightarrow
  \Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)\text{ sober}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{theor:bridge} is a transfer statement. Its substantive input is Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-lattice}; complementation and Lemma~\ref{lem:delete-top} put that theorem into the form needed for Hoare power spaces.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:open-retract}
Let $f:M\to X$ be an open continuous surjection. Then $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)$ is a retract of $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(M)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Define
\[
  s:\mathcal{O}(X)\to\mathcal{O}(M),~ s(U)=f^{-1}(U),
\]
and
\[
  r:\mathcal{O}(M)\to\mathcal{O}(X),~ r(V)=f(V).
\]
The second map is well defined because $f$ is open. Both maps preserve arbitrary unions, hence directed suprema, and are Scott continuous. Surjectivity of $f$ gives
\[
  r(s(U))=f(f^{-1}(U))=U
\]
for every $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$. Therefore $r\circ s=id_{\mathcal{O}(X)}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:transfer-nonsober}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:open-retract}, if $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)$ is not sober, then $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(M)$ is not sober.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theor:countable-ponomarev}
Every countable second-countable $T_{1}$-space is an open continuous image of a countable zero-dimensional metrizable space.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $X$ be countable and second-countable, and let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable base. Regard $\mathcal{B}$ as a discrete space. For a finite sequence
\[
  t=(B_{0},\ldots,B_{k-1})\in\mathcal{B}^{<\mathbb{N}},
\]
put $\bigcap t=X$ when $k=0$ and $\bigcap t=\bigcap_{i<k}B_{i}$ otherwise.

For every pair $(x,t)$ with $x\in\bigcap t$, choose a sequence
\[
  b(x,t)=(B_{n}(x,t))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\mathcal{B}^{\mathbb{N}}
\]
whose first $k$ terms are those of $t$ and whose terms form a neighborhood base at $x$. Such a sequence exists because a second-countable space is first-countable. Set
\[
  M=\{b(x,t):t\in\mathcal{B}^{<\mathbb{N}},\ x\in\bigcap t\}
  \subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\mathbb{N}}.
\]
There are only countably many pairs $(x,t)$, so $M$ is countable. The cylinder sets form a clopen base of $\mathcal{B}^{\mathbb{N}}$; hence $M$ is zero-dimensional and metrizable. For example, the product is metrized by
\[
  d(a,b)=
  \begin{cases}
    0, & a=b,\\
    2^{-\min\{n~\!\!:~\!\!a_{n}\neq b_{n}\}}, & a\neq b.
  \end{cases}
\]

A sequence in $M$ cannot be a neighborhood base at two distinct points. If it were a base at $x\neq y$, then every term would contain both points. The $T_{1}$ open neighborhood $X\setminus\{y\}$ of $x$ would contain one of those terms, a contradiction. We may therefore define
\[
  p:M\to X,~ p(b(x,t))=x.
\]
Taking $t$ to be the empty sequence shows that $p$ is surjective.

For $t=(B_{0},\ldots,B_{k-1})$, let
\[
  [t]=\{a\in\mathcal{B}^{\mathbb{N}}:a_{i}=B_{i}\text{ for }i<k\}.
\]
Then
\[
  p(M\cap[t])=\bigcap t. \tag{1}
\]
The inclusion from left to right holds because every term of a sequence assigned to $x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. The reverse inclusion follows from the presence of $b(x,t)$ for every $x\in\bigcap t$. The sets $M\cap[t]$ form a base of $M$, and (1) shows that $p$ is open.

Finally, let $a=(A_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in M$, let $p(a)=x$, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $x$. Since $(A_{n})$ is a neighborhood base at $x$, there is an $n$ with $A_{n}\subseteq U$. For $t=(A_{0},\ldots,A_{n})$, equation (1) gives
\[
  p(M\cap[t])=\bigcap_{i\leq n}A_{i}\subseteq A_{n}\subseteq U.
\]
Thus $p$ is continuous.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:HZ-input}
There exists a countable second-countable $T_{1}$-space $X$ such that $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)$ is not sober.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Corollary 4.13 of \cite{HeZhao2026} gives a countable $T_{1}$-space that is compact but not $SI$-compact. Lemma 3.5 of the same paper states that, if $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)$ is sober, then compactness and $SI$-compactness are equivalent. Hence the Scott space $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(X)$ of their example is not sober.

It remains only to record a countability property of their topology. The underlying poset $\widehat P$ is countable. Its lower topology is generated by the countable subbase
\[
  \{\widehat P\setminus\mathord{\uparrow}x:x\in\widehat P\}.
\]
The topology in Corollary 4.13 is generated by this lower topology together with the co-finite subsets of $\widehat P$. There are only countably many co-finite subsets of a countable set. The resulting topology therefore has a countable subbase, and is second-countable.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
There exists a countable zero-dimensional metrizable space $M$ such that
\[
  \Sigma\mathcal{O}(M)\text{ is not sober}
  ~\text{and}~
  P_{H}(M)\text{ is not co-sober}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Choose $X$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:HZ-input}. By Theorem~\ref{theor:countable-ponomarev}, there are a countable zero-dimensional metrizable space $M$ and an open continuous surjection $p:M\to X$. Corollary~\ref{cor:transfer-nonsober} shows that $\Sigma\mathcal{O}(M)$ is not sober. Theorem~\ref{theor:bridge} then gives that $P_{H}(M)$ is not co-sober.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
